https://www.theweek.in/news/world/2026/0.text: Influencer brothers Andrew and Tristan Tate, who were popular in the “manosphere” circles, were arrested in Miami on Saturday after fresh charges of rape and sex trafficking were filed in the UK, US and British officials said. The additional charges against Andrew, 39 and Tristan, 38, were brought on by the UK’s Crown Prosecution Service. The agency said that it is awaiting the the brother’s extradition to the UK. Andrew Tate is facing seven additional counts of rape, three counts of arranging or facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation, three counts of assault occasioning actual bodily harm and 19 additional charges relating to illegal child images and pornography. Tristan Tate faces one count of sexual assault, two counts of rape and three counts of arranging or facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation The charges cover alleged offences from July 2010 to August 2017, MBC news reported. The brothers hold dual US and British citizenship. The news charges relate to four additional alleged victims. Previous charges were connected to three alleged victims. The Tates have long denied all criminal allegations against them.  The brother’s lawyer said that the pair 'would walk' free before travelling across the Atlantic, the BBC reported. "We are confident that once a competent judge sees the facts, and once the Department of Justice confronts this egregious abuse of its own authority, Andrew and Tristan Tate will walk free," he said “This is not law enforcement, this is a political hit... America does not do Britain’s political dirty work,” he added. The Tates were both former kickboxers and have been long associated with the manosphere, a social media phenomenon that is anti feminist and which has been accused of promoting toxic masculinity and misogyny. In 2022, they were arrested along with two Romanian women in Bucharest and subsequently indicted. Last year, a Romanian travel ban on the two was lifted, which allowed them to move to the US. The previous allegation included the coercion of a 17-year-old girl into pornography and the rape of a minor. They returned in 2025 and have remained under criminal investigation in Romania on allegations of organised crime, human trafficking, trafficking of minors and money laundering. The Crown Prosecution Service said that the decision to file new charges came after it received new evidence from police in Bedfordshire and neighbouring Hertfordshire County.

https://metro.co.uk/2026/08/28/prankster.text: Polish police arrested a suspected prankster who could end up serving eight years over bogus orders (Pictures: Getty Images) A suspected prankster faces an unappetising eight years in prison after hundreds of unwanted food deliveries were ordered to strangers’ homes. One particularly ambitious request called for 300 pizzas. According to a report by Euronews, the 23-year-old was arrested at his home in northwestern Poland, following an investigation into what authorities are treating as a case of harassment. He’s also suspected of stalking, identity fraud and causing substantial financial losses to restaurants. The orders were placed using other people’s names and were made payable on delivery. That left unsuspecting recipients opening their doors to couriers carrying food they hadn’t requested and expecting them to hand over the dough themselves. Restaurants were cheesed off after being left with hundreds of unwanted and unpaid meals (Picture: Getty Images) Most of the food was supposed to be delivered in the city of Szczecin, but orders were also placed in Warsaw, Kraków and Wrocław. More than a dozen incidents were recorded in those cities combined. One order alone was worth more than 37,000 złoty, or around £7,350. Another called for a kitchen-stretching 300 pizzas, which is less dinner for one and more catering for a micronation for the weekend. Delivery drivers were taken for a ride by bogus orders placed in strangers’ names (Picture: Getty Images) Thankfully for the business, that mammoth order didn’t make it into the oven. Restaurants sometimes rejected requests that were too large to prepare within the specified time, according to investigators. Other businesses weren’t so fortunate and were left with rather hefty losses from unpaid orders. What might have been dismissed as a silly takeaway prank therefore became considerably harder to swallow for those left out of pocket. The orders also carried a much more sinister topping. Authorities say some included detailed information about the intended recipients which could only have been known to them or those closest to them. Orders piled high as the suspected prank grew increasingly hard to swallow (Picture: Getty Images) Police have said that the victims were left feeling threatened and tormented by the apparent intrusions into their private lives. Certain delivery notes reportedly referred to abducting a child, setting fire to a notary’s office and deliberately causing a road accident. At that point, it was less a mozzarella-topped practical joke and more of a genuine suspected campaign of intimidation and harassment. Officers from Poland’s Central Bureau for Combating Cybercrime worked with investigators from Szczecin’s municipal police headquarters to identify a suspect. The operation was supervised by the District Prosecutor’s Office in Szczecin. Szczecin was the main base for the bogus orders before the scheme spread to other Polish cities (Picture: Getty Images) Police detained the man during a raid on his home, although they’re yet to release his name publicly. Electronic devices and data carriers that may have been used to place the orders were seized for examination. He has been remanded in custody for two months while the investigation continues. Authorities haven’t disclosed what they believe motivated the campaign. The suspect hasn’t been convicted and the case against him has yet to be heard in court. If found guilty of the offences under investigation, he could receive a sentence of up to eight years. And that’s a hefty sentence whichever way you slice it.
